newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Serb rape witness accused of lying.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb rape witness accused of lying.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb woman, testifying as a rape witness at a U.N. criminal tribunal, was accused on Monday of lying in her evidence of alleged atrocities at a Moslem/Croat-run detention camp.

Defence lawyers for three Moslems and a Croat on trial for war crimes allegedly committed at the Celebici camp in central Bosnia in 1992 suggested Milojka Antic had fabricated parts of her evidence to tribunal prosecutors in February last year.

"You made those statements without knowing if they were true or not...They were just words on paper," said laywer Thomas Moran, defending counsel for the Moslem deputy commander of the camp, Hazim Delic.

Antic's original testimony detailed a horrific regime of incarceration and repeated sexual assaults in which she accused Delic of raping her vaginally and anally. She said she had been raped every few days for the first seven weeks of her detention.
Her written testimony is detailed in the indictment issued against Delic, in the dock alongside Moslems Zejnil Delalic and Esad Landzo and Croat Zdravko "Pavo" Mucic.
But testifying before open court, 48-year-old Antic said she had been raped three times, and that Delic had once attempted to penetrate her anally but stopped when she screamed with pain.

"Maybe I said something that I didn't know...because I was being reminded of all those moments, those worst moments I lived through," Antic said in response to aggressive cross-examination from Moran, who at one point was reprimanded by judge Adolphus Karibi-Whyte for a style which he said amounted to harassment.

Continuing a similar line of questioning, Mucic's defence counsel Michael Greaves said Antic had invented an episode contained in her oral testimony in which she said Mucic had interrogated her when she arrived at the camp in June 1992.

Testifying before last week's five-day recess, Antic told the court that Mucic, the camp's commander, on discovering she was unmarried had turned to Delic and said: "This is just the right type for you."
"You simply invented it, it didn't happen...it's a lie," Greaves said, pointing out the events were not contained in her original written testimony given to tribunal prosecutors.
"I may have forgotten to mention it, but it's true," Antic replied, speaking impassively in Serbo-Croat.
The trial, now in its fifth week, is the first war crimes hearing by an international body since the Tokyo trials after World War Two to deal with accusations of rape and sexual assault.
The four defendants are jointly accused of responsibility for the murder, rape and toruture of Serb prisoners at the camp.

The indictment issued by the tribunal in March 1996 details acts of torture including beatings with shovels, baseball bats and metal chains, which at times led to death. Acid, gasoline and corrosive powders were also used on prisoners, it alleges.
The U.N. tribunal has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has since died), 18 Croats and three Moslems.

One man, Croat Drazan Erdemovic, who admitted helping to slay thousands of Moslems from Srebrenica, has been convicted and sentenced to 10 years in jail. A verdict in the case of Bosnian Serb Dusan "Dusko" Tadic is expected soon.
The two most prominent indicted suspects are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
